prompt: A packet becomes twice as large while its link rate also doubles. Ignore overhead and keep the route and medium unchanged. What happens to transmission delay?

options.text: It halves, because the link is faster
options.explanation: The faster link is also sending twice as many bits; both changes matter.
Correct. Twice as many bits sent at twice the bit rate takes the same transmission time.

options.text: It doubles, because the packet is larger
options.explanation: That ignores the matching increase in link rate.

options.text: It depends only on cable length
options.explanation: Cable length affects propagation delay; this question isolates putting all bits onto the link.

workedExample: Separate the two effects. Doubling packet size alone would take twice as long to send. Doubling the rate then sends those bits twice as quickly. The effects cancel for transmission delay. Propagation stays unchanged because route and medium were held fixed.

prompt: A user expects a 100 Mbit/s link to deliver a file at 100 MB/s. Which explanation addresses the expectation correctly?

options.text: The units are equivalent; any smaller number proves a fault
options.explanation: A bit and a byte are different quantities, so the displayed numbers cannot be compared directly.

options.text: A byte contains eight bits, and protocol overhead can lower useful file rate further
options.explanation: Correct. Convert the units before comparing rates, then account for the chosen payload boundary and other limits.

options.text: Every internet transfer loses exactly 5% to overhead
options.explanation: Overhead depends on packet sizes, headers, protocols and retransmissions; there is no fixed universal percentage.

options.text: The cable length changes how many bits are in a byte
options.explanation: Distance changes propagation time, not the eight-bit byte conversion.

workedExample: First compare like units: the advertised rate counts bits per second, while the file display counts bytes per second. Then distinguish raw capacity from useful application data. Headers, setup, congestion, server and host limits may reduce the file rate; a number below the raw label does not by itself locate a fault.
